transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
Cornell University has suspended parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic
year, among other changes in response to a student's allegations of gang rape in October
2024, NPR's Alyssa Nadwurni reports.
The university announced a number of changes to strengthen campus safety and better support
sexual assault survivors.
In addition to banning all parties and social events at fraternity houses, the Ivy League
school will also hire staff to help students navigate reporting sexual misconduct and will
hire criminal investigators, independent of Cornell, to investigate allegations of sexual
assault on campus.
In a letter to the campus, the school's president, Michael Kotlikoff, writes, "Cornell must
be a place where safety is not an open question.
The changes come amid continued frustration and protests from students and faculty on the
handling of Jane Doe's 2024 case."
Alyssa Nadwurni, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
The Supreme Court will hear a dispute over a watchdog group's effort to get information
about the Department of Government Efficiency, also known as Doge.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports a lower court found Doge is likely covered by the Freedom
of Information Act.
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington demanded information about Doge, the agency
affiliated with Elon Musk, that worked to reshape the federal government.
Crew officials wanted to know about Doge's operations and its role in job cuts.
A federal judge in Washington sided with the watchdog group, but the Trump administration
called Doge an advisory panel, not subject to a Freedom of Information law.
The high court granted the administration some relief on the emergency docket.
Now it will consider the issues more fully.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
The Trump administration is cutting the time refugees have to contest the termination of
their status.
Critics say the move could put tens of thousands of people who fled persecution and wars in
their home countries on a path to deportation.
The new policy is part of a broader effort to restrict the program that has served for
decades as a pathway to safety for refugees.
New research from the AI company Anthropics suggests that some AI might soon be able to
replicate inside smart devices, NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports.
Anthropics warned that AI models could soon spread inside network devices around the house,
including smart refrigerators, televisions, and even robotic vacuum cleaners.
Researchers demonstrated such replication inside some cheap TV boxes and with simulations.
The researchers warned AI worms would be similar to existing computer viruses, but they would
be more adaptable and could be hard to shut down.
The best defense against AI and regular viruses alike?
A strong password for every smart device in your home.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
Major U.S. stock indexes closed down today.
The S&P 500 edged down a fraction.
The Dow fell more than a quarter percent.
This is NPR News.
The Army is deploying hundreds of soldiers to Texas's Rio Grande Valley in response to
what it says is elevated activity from drug cartels.
Rio also has sent hundreds of troops to the border to coordinate with the U.S.
The Army has been inviting reporters to see the area that was once the epicenter of illegal
crossings to showcase its progress in stemming the flow.
Some experts questioned the need for the surge, saying it's more for show just weeks before
the midterm elections.
Nine more roller coasters across the U.S. and Canada are temporarily closed after an
accident at Six Flags Over Georgia left one man dead.
Melissa Phato from member station W.A.B.E. has more.
Police say their preliminary investigation shows a 42-year-old man was thrown from the
ride and struck other riders before falling beneath the attraction, killing him.
Investigators are still examining what led to the accident.
Authorities did not identify the ride, but local TV footage showed riders being evacuated
from the 200-foot hypercoaster Goliath Monday afternoon.
All but one of the other coasters now closed across the chain are, like Goliath, manufactured
by Swiss company Bolliger & Mabelard.
Six Flags says they've done so out of an abundance of caution.
This comes as the company has faced financial struggles and leadership changes after merging
with its once-competitor, Cedar Fair, in 2024.
For NPR News, I'm Melissa Phato in Atlanta.
A Rhode Island pumpkin grower appears to have set a new world record for the heaviest pumpkin.
Ron Wallace's giant squash weighed in at 3,156 pounds at a contest in New England.
It's about the weight of an adult hippopotamus.
This is NPR News.
